measureRecords.whatItDoes: Approves Danbury’s other charter revisions as one package, covering city finances, school financial reporting, appointments, Council procedures, ward redistricting and department organization. Among the changes, the threshold requiring a public vote on bond or note borrowing would rise from $3 million to $5 million in total authorizations in a fiscal year; existing emergency and benefit-assessed sewer and water extension exceptions would remain. The Mayor could accept gifts totaling up to $5,000 from one donor in a fiscal year, rather than $1,000, except where state law provides otherwise, and report them at the next regular Council meeting; larger gifts would go to the Council for acceptance at its next special or regular meeting. On the Mayor’s request, the Council could transfer uncommitted appropriations between departments throughout the year, removing the current restriction to the last four months; appropriations for debt service and other statutory charges could not be transferred. The report removes the rule automatically treating a capital project as abandoned after three fiscal years without spending or a commitment of funds, and the accompanying year-end lapse clause for unused annual appropriations. It replaces mandatory removal for an officer’s or employee’s knowing charter violation in incurring obligations or spending with possible progressive discipline determined by the department head or Mayor and Human Resources. The Mayor would present the annual budget at the Council’s first regular meeting in April instead of by April 7 or the next business day. A new school-board section would apply city accounting, auditing and reporting procedures to school finances while preserving the school board’s legal authority over educational policies, programs and internal management. The school board would give the Mayor and Finance Department access to school financial books, accounts, records, contracts and spending data solely for auditing, budgeting and financial reporting, excluding protected student data and education records. For timely audits, the Superintendent could give a designated city finance employee access to the school financial system with privacy safeguards; the changes would not authorize city officials to direct school educational operations. The school board’s complete annual financial report would go to the Mayor and Council promptly after the year-end report is submitted to the state Education Department, by September 30, replacing the August 15 deadline. The Council’s power to disapprove the Mayor’s Chief of Staff appointment would be removed. The Mayor’s Legislative Assistant nominee would need confirmation by two-thirds of the entire Council, rather than two-thirds of those present and voting, and meet added administrative qualifications; the Mayor could remove that assistant unless two-thirds of the entire Council disapprove at its next meeting. For an elected-office vacancy other than the school board, if the Council fails to appoint a replacement within 60 days, the Mayor would appoint one within the next 30 days; the same-party replacement rule would continue when the departing official was elected as a party member. Three of the first four ward-redistricting commission members could select the fifth member instead of needing unanimity; if they do not do so within 30 days, the Mayor would nominate the fifth member for Council confirmation. The Council could establish and end standing committees by resolution, alongside temporary committees and meetings as a committee of the whole. The charter would create a Technology Services Department responsible for city information systems and cybersecurity, and update department names, appointment language and other references.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve the package of other proposed charter revisions, including the financial, school-reporting, appointment and Council changes described here.
measureRecords.noMeans: Reject this package of other proposed charter revisions.
